sections.body: The pick swap widened Philadelphia’s advantage. Denver received the No. 21 selection in 1978 and used it on Mike Evans, a legitimate NBA guard. Philadelphia later received the No. 10 pick in 1984 and selected Leon Wood. Wood did not become a star, so the draft component should not be exaggerated, but it gave the 76ers another first-round asset after Jones had already delivered years of elite play. Ralph Simpson contributed only briefly. The transaction’s value remains centered on Jones and McGinnis, with the draft outcomes reinforcing rather than creating the verdict. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first / George McGinnis and Mike Evans: Verdict and Grade Calibration
sections.body: The old Partner Win label identified the correct side but obscured the franchise and treated Denver too harshly. The revised verdict is 76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A-plus because Jones became a championship pillar and one of the era’s best defenders while accepting roles that unlocked the rest of the roster. Denver rises from F to B-minus because McGinnis remained an All-Star and Evans had a useful career. A losing team can receive a productive star and still lose when the other side acquires a longer-lasting, better-fitting Hall of Fame contributor. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict

Denver still earns a B-minus for an All-Star season from George McGinnis and useful years from Mike Evans, but the return was shorter and less portable.

sections.heading: Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first / George McGinnis and Mike Evans: Control and Durability
sections.body: Philadelphia controlled Jones from age 26 through the end of his career. That gave the organization eight seasons of role stability across Finals teams, coaching adjustments and the arrival of Moses Malone. Denver controlled McGinnis for less than two seasons before moving him, and injury reduced the value of the period it did hold. Evans supplied longer service, but as a secondary guard rather than a foundational piece. The difference in control is not merely chronological. Jones’s presence allowed Philadelphia to make other aggressive decisions because the defense and connective play were dependable every season. Durability includes contractual control, repeated role stability and the ability to build subsequent rosters around the return. A shorter brilliant window can beat longer average service, but the years still matter.

sections.heading: Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first / George McGinnis and Mike Evans: Postseason Translation
sections.body: Jones played in three Finals with Philadelphia and was central to the 1983 championship. His defense, transition speed and ability to contribute without plays being called for him translated cleanly against elite postseason opponents. McGinnis missed the 1979 playoffs after the ankle injury, and Denver did not produce a comparable run from the trade. Evans later appeared in postseason games, but the competitive gap remained large. Philadelphia’s return passed the hardest test repeatedly: Jones remained useful when possessions slowed, matchups tightened and star teammates needed complementary impact rather than another high-usage scorer. Playoff results are evidence rather than the only test. They reveal whether a skill set survives scouting, pressure and slower possessions and should be credited only to the team that received the player in this transaction.

sections.heading: Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first / George McGinnis and Mike Evans: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: Denver’s best counterfactual is a healthy McGinnis sustaining his first-season form. At the time, acquiring an established star for a defense-first forward could be defended, especially for a franchise seeking identity after the merger. Philadelphia’s risk was that Jones’s limited self-creation would leave the offense short of scoring. Instead, his low-maintenance style amplified Erving and later Malone. The lesson is not that teams should always choose defense over scoring. It is that fit, age and role elasticity can make the quieter player more valuable when the roster already has primary offense. Counterfactuals are most useful when they describe realistic alternatives available at the time. They are least useful when they assume knowledge or offers the market never supplied.

sections.heading: Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first / George McGinnis and Mike Evans: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: Jones became one of the most beloved and respected 76ers, a Hall of Famer whose career is often used to explain the value of defense and selflessness. McGinnis remains a Hall of Fame talent and an important figure in both ABA and NBA history, which is why Denver should not be reduced to a punch line. The trade’s legacy is Philadelphia’s ability to exchange a bigger individual name for the player its roster actually needed. A-plus versus B-minus recognizes that the Nuggets received real production while the 76ers received the enduring championship piece. Legacy compresses years into a familiar story, but the grade remains tied to direct production, downstream conversion, contract value and the competitive identity created by the return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Philadelphia wins because Bobby Jones delivered eight seasons of elite defense, role flexibility, All-Star value and a central place on the 1983 champions. Denver still earns a B-minus for an All-Star season from George McGinnis and useful years from Mike Evans, but the return was shorter and less portable.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On May 23, 1975, Boston sent Paul Westphal and two second-round picks to Phoenix for Charlie Scott. Westphal had spent three seasons behind an established Celtics backcourt and was not yet a full-time star. Scott was already a proven scorer who could help a veteran Boston team immediately. The transaction therefore exchanged a younger guard with unrealized upside for a more established scorer aligned with the Celtics’ championship window. Phoenix gained both player development opportunity and draft depth, while Boston gained the player it believed could replace some of the scoring and creation lost as its roster aged. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Phoenix’s edge comes from Westphal’s development into one of the league’s best guards. He made four consecutive All-Star teams as a Sun, earned four straight All-NBA selections and averaged more than 20 points for five consecutive seasons. His ambidextrous finishing, midrange skill, playmaking and late-game intelligence became central to the franchise. In his first Phoenix season, Westphal helped lead a 42-win team through an improbable playoff run to the 1976 Finals against Boston. The Suns received a Hall of Fame player during his prime and controlled six productive seasons before his first departure. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Boston’s return was also excellent. Scott averaged 17.6 points in his first Celtics season and started for the team that won the 1976 championship. His ability to create offense from the wing reduced pressure on John Havlicek and Jo Jo White, and he remained a double-figure scorer during three Boston seasons. The tenure was shorter and the individual peak lower than Westphal’s Phoenix run, but a championship starter acquired for a blocked young guard is a major success. An A-minus reflects the direct title value and prevents the verdict from becoming a hindsight-driven condemnation of Red Auerbach’s decision. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Boston was defending a title-era core and prioritizing immediate fit. Westphal had talent, but White and Havlicek occupied the primary perimeter roles. Phoenix could offer the ball, minutes and freedom that allowed his game to expand. Scott, meanwhile, had already been a high-volume scorer and was better prepared to contribute to Boston’s existing system. The teams were not choosing between the same versions of the players. Phoenix bought future growth; Boston bought present reliability. Both objectives were achieved, which is why the final margin should remain slight despite Westphal’s stronger career outcome. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The two second-round picks did not materially alter the trade. Phoenix used them on Jimmy Dan Conner and Raymond Feher, neither of whom became an important NBA contributor. The ledger therefore reduces almost entirely to Westphal versus Scott. That direct comparison favors Phoenix in peak, years and individual recognition, but Boston’s championship converts Scott’s shorter stay into unusually valuable team impact. The trade is a reminder that additional draft assets should be followed to their actual outcomes rather than counted as automatic surplus. Here, the picks were peripheral and the two guards carried the verdict. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Verdict and Grade Calibration
sections.body: The old Slight Partner Edge label was directionally sound but unnecessarily generic, and the grades understated both teams. The revised verdict is Slight Suns Edge. Phoenix rises to A because it received a Hall of Fame guard in his prime and the leader of its first Finals team. Boston rises to A-minus because Scott was a high-level starter on a champion. The single-step grade difference captures the true shape: Phoenix won the longer individual-value comparison, while Boston accomplished the exact championship objective that justified trading future upside. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix earns a slight edge because Paul Westphal became a four-time All-Star, four-time All-NBA guard and the leader of the Suns’ first Finals team. Boston still earns an A-minus because Charlie Scott immediately became a major scorer and starter on the 1976 champions.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Peak Impact
sections.body: Westphal’s Phoenix peak was elite. He combined efficient scoring, playmaking and improvisation while earning first-team All-NBA recognition three times. His quick thinking in the famous triple-overtime Game 5 of the 1976 Finals became part of league history. Scott’s Boston peak was lower individually but still substantial: he was a dynamic scorer and starter on a 54-win champion. Westphal’s ability to serve as the primary perimeter engine creates the edge, yet Scott’s championship-level role keeps the comparison from becoming lopsided. Peak seasons matter because high-impact players alter matchups, roster construction and postseason ceilings in ways that ordinary cumulative minutes do not.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Control and Durability
sections.body: Phoenix controlled Westphal for five consecutive prime seasons before trading him in 1980, then later brought him back. Those years included the franchise’s first Finals appearance and repeated All-NBA production. Boston controlled Scott for three seasons, all during the closing phase of its Havlicek-Cowens contention window. The Celtics received the concentrated value they sought, but the Suns received both a longer runway and a player whose role expanded over time. Control favored Phoenix because Westphal’s best seasons were still ahead when the trade occurred, while Scott’s Boston value was immediate and finite. Durability includes contractual control, repeated role stability and the ability to build subsequent rosters around the return. A shorter brilliant window can beat longer average service, but the years still matter.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Postseason Translation
sections.body: The 1976 Finals makes the trade uniquely balanced. Scott helped Boston win the championship, while Westphal was arguably Phoenix’s most important offensive player in pushing the series to six games. Both returns translated directly to the same Finals stage one year after the transaction. Boston owns the ring, which matters greatly, but Phoenix’s run was the first in franchise history and Westphal remained a star after it ended. The postseason record supports strong grades on both sides and a slight Phoenix edge rather than either an even label or a decisive Suns win. Playoff results are evidence rather than the only test. They reveal whether a skill set survives scouting, pressure and slower possessions and should be credited only to the team that received the player in this transaction.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: Boston’s counterfactual is whether Westphal would have reached the same peak behind White and Havlicek. He may not have received enough creation responsibility before the veteran core declined. Phoenix’s risk was giving up an established scorer for a guard who had never averaged even ten points in Boston. The Suns correctly identified that opportunity, not merely talent, was suppressing Westphal’s value. The Celtics correctly identified that Scott could help immediately. Because both teams solved a real roster problem, the result should be judged as a rare trade in which one side’s long-term edge coexists with the other side’s championship success. Counterfactuals are most useful when they describe realistic alternatives available at the time. They are least useful when they assume knowledge or offers the market never supplied.

sections.heading: Paul Westphal and two second-round picks / Charlie Scott: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: Westphal became one of the defining figures in Suns history as both a player and later a coach. Scott’s Celtics tenure is remembered most for the 1976 title and his fit within one of the franchise’s classic teams. The trade’s legacy is therefore richer than a winner-loser slogan. Phoenix discovered a Hall of Fame centerpiece; Boston converted surplus backcourt potential into another championship starter. An A for the Suns and A-minus for the Celtics preserves the small difference in total value without rewriting a mutually successful transaction as a disaster for either organization. Legacy compresses years into a familiar story, but the grade remains tied to direct production, downstream conversion, contract value and the competitive identity created by the return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Phoenix earns a slight edge because Paul Westphal became a four-time All-Star, four-time All-NBA guard and the leader of the Suns’ first Finals team. Boston still earns an A-minus because Charlie Scott immediately became a major scorer and starter on the 1976 champions.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On December 24, 1981, the Los Angeles Lakers acquired Bob McAdoo’s rights from the New Jersey Nets for cash and a 1983 second-round pick that became Kevin Williams at No. 46. McAdoo was a former MVP and scoring champion, but foot surgery, a contract dispute and several recent team changes had depressed his market. The Lakers needed frontcourt scoring after Mitch Kupchak suffered a major knee injury. New Jersey chose a small asset return over continuing the standoff. Los Angeles was not paying a superstar price; it was betting that a historically great scorer would accept a reduced role on a contender. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: McAdoo made the bet work immediately. He came off the bench, supplied efficient scoring and averaged 16.7 points during the 1982 playoffs as the Lakers won the championship. He remained a key reserve through four seasons, appeared in three additional Finals and won another title in 1985. His ability to score against second units and play alongside either Kareem Abdul-Jabbar or a smaller frontcourt gave Pat Riley tactical flexibility. The Lakers received meaningful production during multiple title runs for a second-round pick and cash, an acquisition-cost-to-impact ratio worthy of an A-plus. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: The Nets’ return produced almost no lasting basketball value. Kevin Williams played only a brief NBA career and did not become a rotation piece capable of offsetting McAdoo’s contribution. Cash may have helped resolve the contract dispute, but it did not create an identifiable downstream asset in the canonical record. New Jersey faced legitimate leverage problems because McAdoo was not playing and wanted a different situation. Even so, converting a former MVP’s rights into a marginal second-round outcome left the franchise with neither immediate production nor future control. An F reflects the realized return rather than punishing the Nets simply for the existence of the dispute. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: The Lakers could absorb risks that most teams could not. Their roster already had Magic Johnson, Abdul-Jabbar, Jamaal Wilkes and Norm Nixon, so McAdoo did not need to recreate his Buffalo scoring volume. He needed to accept bench minutes, attack favorable matchups and support a championship rotation. The Nets lacked comparable leverage because the player’s contract and health circumstances limited the market. Los Angeles’s advantage was organizational credibility: McAdoo could believe that sacrificing starts would produce the championship opportunity missing from his career. The trade became a model for acquiring distressed veteran talent into a clearly defined role. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The asset ledger is direct. Williams, the player selected with the outgoing second, did not produce meaningful Nets value. McAdoo delivered four Lakers seasons, high-level playoff scoring and two championships. Los Angeles did not later convert him into another asset when he left, but the team had already extracted the purpose of the transaction. This is an example in which terminal value is acceptable because the competitive return was fully realized. The Nets’ cash and pick did not compound, while the Lakers’ acquired player converted immediately into wins at the highest level. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Verdict and Grade Calibration
sections.body: The old Partner Win label should be replaced by Lakers Win, and the grades need a wider spread. Los Angeles rises from A-minus to A-plus because McAdoo’s 1982 playoff performance and second championship in 1985 far exceeded the acquisition cost. New Jersey falls from D-plus to F because the pick and cash yielded no meaningful on-court return. The verdict is not based solely on McAdoo’s pre-trade reputation. It follows from what he actually did for the Lakers after the deal and what the Nets actually realized from the assets they accepted. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Lakers win because Bob McAdoo became a major playoff scorer, accepted a crucial reserve role and contributed to the 1982 and 1985 championships. The Nets received only cash and a second-round pick that produced negligible NBA value, leaving no durable counterweight.

featuredDeepDive.intro: The transaction is best understood by following the actual assets, the roles available on each roster and the years of control that followed. This deep dive tests Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash across peak value, durability, postseason use, realistic alternatives and historical legacy.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Peak Impact
sections.body: McAdoo’s Lakers peak came during the 1982 postseason, when he provided starter-level scoring from a reserve role and repeatedly punished opposing benches. He no longer carried an offense as he had during his MVP years, but the narrower role made his scoring more efficient and strategically valuable. The Nets’ peak return was essentially the option to use a mid-second-round pick. Williams never approached a regular rotation role. The peak comparison is therefore extreme: one side received championship-level playoff offense, while the other received almost no NBA production. Peak seasons matter because high-impact players alter matchups, roster construction and postseason ceilings in ways that ordinary cumulative minutes do not.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Control and Durability
sections.body: Los Angeles retained McAdoo for four seasons and reached the Finals in each one. That continuity allowed Riley to define a stable sixth-man role and manage an aging frontcourt without asking McAdoo to be the franchise centerpiece. New Jersey controlled the draft pick but received little value after using it. The Lakers’ control was especially valuable because McAdoo chose to re-sign despite other options, extending the benefit beyond the initial half-season. Years alone do not guarantee value; in this case, four years overlapped perfectly with a championship window and multiplied the return. Durability includes contractual control, repeated role stability and the ability to build subsequent rosters around the return. A shorter brilliant window can beat longer average service, but the years still matter.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Postseason Translation
sections.body: Few low-cost acquisitions translated more directly to postseason success. McAdoo averaged 16.7 points in the 1982 playoffs and 16.3 in the Finals, giving the Lakers a scoring weapon that Philadelphia could not match off the bench. He later contributed to the 1985 title that ended Los Angeles’s long Finals frustration against Boston. The Nets received no postseason value from Williams connected to the transaction. The two rings should not be credited to one reserve alone, but they are strong evidence that McAdoo’s skill survived playoff pressure and filled a real championship need. Playoff results are evidence rather than the only test. They reveal whether a skill set survives scouting, pressure and slower possessions and should be credited only to the team that received the player in this transaction.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: The Best Counterfactual
sections.body: New Jersey’s strongest defense is leverage. McAdoo was injured, unhappy and unavailable, so a rich market may not have existed. Holding his rights longer could have produced nothing and prolonged the dispute. The Lakers’ risk was that his foot problems or resistance to a bench role would destabilize the roster. Instead, McAdoo embraced the opportunity. The lesson is that distressed stars can create enormous asymmetry when the acquiring team has a credible role, medical plan and championship incentive. The Nets’ process was constrained, but the realized return remains an F. Counterfactuals are most useful when they describe realistic alternatives available at the time. They are least useful when they assume knowledge or offers the market never supplied.

sections.heading: Bob McAdoo / second-round pick and cash: Legacy and Final Accounting
sections.body: McAdoo’s Lakers chapter changed how his career is remembered. He had already been an MVP and one of the greatest scorers of the 1970s, yet the move proved he could sacrifice status and become a championship reserve. The Nets are a footnote in that story because the return disappeared quickly. For Los Angeles, the trade became another example of turning a modest asset into a Hall of Fame contributor at exactly the right moment. A-plus versus F captures both the tiny price and the repeated championship payoff. Legacy compresses years into a familiar story, but the grade remains tied to direct production, downstream conversion, contract value and the competitive identity created by the return.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Lakers win because Bob McAdoo became a major playoff scorer, accepted a crucial reserve role and contributed to the 1982 and 1985 championships. The Nets received only cash and a second-round pick that produced negligible NBA value, leaving no durable counterweight.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson / Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, picks and cash: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On February 13, 1987, Los Angeles acquired Mychal Thompson from San Antonio for Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, a first-round asset, a future second-round pick and cash. The Lakers had pursued another large, skilled frontcourt player to support Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and withstand matchups against Boston and other contenders. Thompson had joined the Spurs only months earlier and was a proven scorer capable of playing center or power forward. San Antonio accepted a broad package rather than one premium centerpiece. Los Angeles paid real quantity, but it was buying a specific playoff solution during an active championship window. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson / Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, picks and cash: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Thompson’s value appeared immediately. He could defend opposing centers, score on the block or from midrange and allow Abdul-Jabbar to play fewer punishing minutes. The Lakers won the 1987 title after his arrival and repeated in 1988, with Thompson functioning as one of the league’s most capable reserve big men. He remained through the 1991 Finals and played nearly every regular-season game during the core of his tenure. Los Angeles did not acquire an All-Star version of Thompson; it acquired a high-end role player whose size and versatility solved a championship problem. That is an A-level outcome. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson / Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, picks and cash: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: San Antonio received useful but fragmented value. Brickowski became a capable NBA big, though much of his best work came after leaving the Spurs. Gudmundsson provided short-term center minutes. The first-round component was tied to Wayne “Cadillac” Anderson, and the later second became Sean Higgins. None became a durable Spurs starter or a central part of the franchise’s next competitive core. The package was large enough to avoid an F, but the conversion was weak. A C recognizes that several legitimate assets arrived while acknowledging that the Spurs failed to turn them into sustained team value. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson / Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, picks and cash: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: The Lakers’ urgency was rational. Abdul-Jabbar was 39, and the team’s path to another championship required frontcourt depth that could survive playoff matchups without shrinking the offense. Thompson’s experience and positional flexibility made him more valuable to Los Angeles than to a rebuilding Spurs team. San Antonio was years away from drafting David Robinson and had reason to prefer multiple assets. The outcome separated because the Lakers knew exactly what role they were buying, while the Spurs’ return depended on several uncertain conversions. Clarity of role reduced Los Angeles’s risk even though the package looked substantial on paper. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson / Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, picks and cash: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The first-round component requires careful treatment because the canonical record ties it to Anderson rather than a future star. Anderson had a short NBA career, Higgins became a journeyman and the veteran players did not create a major downstream chain for San Antonio. Thompson’s value, by contrast, was consumed directly through championships and repeated Finals appearances. Los Angeles did not need resale value because the competitive objective was immediate and achieved. The ledger therefore favors concentrated realized value over a collection of pieces whose theoretical upside never became a lasting Spurs asset. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Mychal Thompson / Frank Brickowski, Petur Gudmundsson, picks and cash: Verdict and Grade Calibration
sections.body: The old Slight Lakers Edge label understates how decisively the transaction served Los Angeles’s objective. The Lakers won two straight championships with Thompson occupying a meaningful frontcourt role and retained him for multiple additional runs. San Antonio’s B-plus was too generous for a package that produced no comparable starter or future cornerstone. The revised calibration is Lakers Win, Los Angeles A and San Antonio C. The Lakers stop short of A-plus because they paid several assets for a role player rather than acquiring a franchise star, but the team result was unmistakably strong. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: The Lakers win because Mychal Thompson immediately solved a frontcourt need, played a major reserve role on the 1987 and 1988 champions and remained dependable through multiple Finals runs. San Antonio received several assets, but none became a comparable long-term Spurs contributor.

sections.heading: Mario Elie / the second-round pick used on Don Reid: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On August 2, 1993, Houston sent a 1995 second-round pick to Portland for Mario Elie. The pick eventually landed at No. 58 and was used on Don Reid. Elie had been a useful wing for the Trail Blazers, but Portland was clearing room and flexibility to pursue center Chris Dudley. Houston had just won 55 games and needed toughness, shooting and perimeter defense around Hakeem Olajuwon. The transaction looked modest because it involved a role player and a distant late pick. Its importance grew through the exact way Elie’s skills fit Houston’s playoff demands. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Mario Elie / the second-round pick used on Don Reid: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Elie became a central member of the Rockets’ championship supporting cast. He defended larger wings, moved the ball, attacked closeouts and made open threes without needing high usage. Houston won the 1994 title in his first season and repeated in 1995. His “Kiss of Death” three in Game 7 against Phoenix became one of the franchise’s defining shots, and he started throughout the 1995 Finals while averaging efficient double-figure scoring. The Rockets received five seasons of reliable two-way play and postseason nerve for the last pick of a later draft. That conversion is worthy of an A-plus. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Mario Elie / the second-round pick used on Don Reid: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Portland’s return was the No. 58 pick in 1995, used on Don Reid. Reid had a respectable NBA career, primarily as a reserve big in Detroit and Orlando, but he did not play for the Trail Blazers. Portland therefore received almost no team-specific basketball value from the transaction. The decision did create roster flexibility in the short term, and the organization was trying to reshape a veteran team. That context keeps the grade at D rather than treating the move as inexplicable. The direct outcome, however, was a late pick that produced no Portland contribution in exchange for a future championship role player. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Mario Elie / the second-round pick used on Don Reid: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Houston’s roster made Elie more valuable than his raw statistics suggested. Olajuwon drew defensive attention, and the Rockets needed wings willing to defend, shoot and remain composed when playoff possessions became physical. Rudy Tomjanovich trusted veterans who understood spacing and could survive without the ball. Portland was transitioning from its early-1990s Finals core and prioritized other roster moves. The trade separated because Houston offered a defined role on a contender and Elie’s competitive temperament matched it perfectly. The Rockets did not discover a hidden primary scorer; they identified a complementary player whose skills scaled in high-leverage games. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Mario Elie / the second-round pick used on Don Reid: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The outgoing pick’s conversion is important. Because Don Reid became a legitimate NBA player, the pick was not inherently worthless. Portland simply did not retain or realize that player value through the transaction. Houston consumed Elie’s value directly during two championships and later five total seasons. No downstream trade chain is needed to justify the grade. The comparison is a long-tenured championship wing against a draft asset that produced no Blazers minutes. That asymmetry explains why Houston rises from B to A-plus and why Portland’s partner aggregate should match its D. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Mario Elie / the second-round pick used on Don Reid: Verdict and Grade Calibration
sections.body: The Rockets Win verdict remains correct, but the grades need recalibration. Houston’s B treated Elie as an ordinary rotation success rather than a player whose defense, shooting and clutch postseason moments helped secure two titles. A-plus reflects the extraordinary return on a No. 58-level asset. Portland moves from D-plus to D and the partner aggregate is aligned to the actual Blazers result. The loss is not an F because the original pick had some legitimate value and roster flexibility was part of the decision, but the realized gap is still enormous. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Houston wins because Mario Elie became a five-season two-way pillar, contributed to consecutive championships and delivered one of the franchise’s defining playoff shots. Portland received a late second-round pick that produced no meaningful Blazers value, creating a decisive gap.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On February 21, 2013, Orlando traded J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith to Milwaukee for Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih, Doron Lamb and cash. The Bucks were 26-28 and chasing a playoff berth with Brandon Jennings and Monta Ellis. Redick offered shooting and another experienced guard. Harris was only 20 and had not secured a consistent Milwaukee role. Orlando was rebuilding after the Dwight Howard era and could prioritize developmental upside over immediate wins. The transaction therefore exchanged a proven short-term specialist for a young forward whose scoring and positional size had not yet been fully tested. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Harris immediately showed why Orlando valued the gamble. He averaged 17.3 points after the trade, expanded his creation role and developed into a versatile forward capable of scoring inside, from midrange and beyond the arc. Across three Magic seasons he became the best player in the transaction and a credible long-term building block. Orlando later traded him to Detroit for a poor return, but that separate decision does not erase the value acquired in 2013. The Magic turned an expiring veteran into a young starter with substantial market value and multiple productive seasons, supporting an A-plus for this specific trade. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Milwaukee received only a brief Redick tenure. He appeared in 28 regular-season games, the Bucks finished 38-44 and Miami swept them in the first round. Redick then left in a sign-and-trade that did not recover a Harris-level asset. Ayon and Smith had minor roles and did not change the team’s ceiling. The Bucks’ logic was understandable—shooting could help a crowded guard rotation—but the competitive target was too modest to justify surrendering a young player with years of control. An F reflects both the short stay and the failure to preserve value after the playoff push ended. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: The trade illustrates the danger of paying a future-asset price for a marginal win-now objective. Milwaukee was not one veteran away from championship contention. It was trying to secure a low playoff seed, which limited the upside even if Redick played well. Orlando had the opposite incentive: minutes and patience were available, allowing Harris to explore a broader offensive role. The result was not solely a scouting miracle. Opportunity was part of the asset. The Magic could create value because their timeline matched Harris’s development, while the Bucks’ timeline demanded immediate results from a player nearing free agency. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: Udrih and Lamb were secondary pieces, and cash did not drive the verdict. Harris carried almost all of Orlando’s realized value. Redick carried Milwaukee’s side, with Ayon and Smith providing limited depth. The later Harris-to-Detroit trade should be evaluated on its own page; importing that mistake here would confuse acquisition value with later asset management. At the end of this transaction’s direct window, Orlando had obtained the youngest, best and most valuable player. Milwaukee had used its return for a short first-round exit and then watched the primary acquisition leave. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Tobias Harris, Beno Udrih and Doron Lamb / J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith: Verdict and Grade Calibration

Milwaukee remains F, while the partner aggregate is corrected from A to A-plus so it matches the Magic’s actual grade. The verdict does not claim Harris became a superstar in Orlando. It recognizes that the Bucks traded away a valuable young starter for a rental that did not materially improve the postseason outcome. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

Orlando did not reach the postseason during Harris’s tenure, a limitation that should be acknowledged, but team context was rebuilding rather than contention. Harris went on to play for several teams and earn major contracts, but the Magic deserve credit only for the seasons and value they controlled. sections.heading: Kevin Duckworth / Walter Berry: The Deal’s Actual Shape
sections.body: On December 18, 1986, Portland traded rookie forward Walter Berry to San Antonio for rookie center Kevin Duckworth. Berry had been the No. 14 pick and the reigning national college player of the year, while Duckworth had been selected in the second round at No. 33. Portland was dealing with injuries and uncertainty at center and wanted more size. San Antonio pursued the more celebrated prospect and a player whose scoring reputation was far stronger. At the moment of the deal, the Spurs appeared to be acquiring the higher-upside name. Portland instead identified the player whose body type, touch and role would fit its next contender. A useful historical review has to keep the original trade date in view. The clubs were buying different timelines, and the later result should be measured against those timelines rather than against a fictional market with perfect information.

sections.heading: Kevin Duckworth / Walter Berry: The Winning Team’s Case
sections.body: Duckworth developed rapidly after injuries opened a starting role. He won Most Improved Player in 1987-88, made the All-Star team in 1989 and again in 1991, and became a dependable scoring center beside Clyde Drexler, Terry Porter and Buck Williams. Portland reached the Finals in 1990 and 1992 and won 63 games in 1990-91. Duckworth’s midrange touch and interior size gave the offense a different dimension, while his durability stabilized a position repeatedly affected by Sam Bowie’s injuries. The Trail Blazers received six-plus prime seasons and later traded him for Harvey Grant, extending the asset value. The winning grade follows from the player’s actual role, the seasons controlled by the acquiring team and the competitive outcomes that occurred while that team held the asset. Reputation by itself is not enough.

sections.heading: Kevin Duckworth / Walter Berry: The Return Package Deserves a Fair Reading
sections.body: Berry scored effectively in stretches for San Antonio but appeared in only 64 games after the trade and was out of the NBA by 1988. His defense, conditioning and relationship with coaches limited the tenure, and the Spurs did not receive a meaningful downstream asset when he left. The original decision was understandable because Berry had been a dominant college player and a lottery pick only months earlier. Retrospective grading, however, must follow what San Antonio actually received. The short stay and absence of later value support an F even though the acquisition was not irrational at the time. Respecting the losing side matters because trade grading is not a morality play. Useful veteran seasons, draft control and credible roster fit retain value even when the other team receives the larger prize.

sections.heading: Kevin Duckworth / Walter Berry: Leverage and Timing Changed the Price
sections.body: Portland’s roster problem created opportunity. The organization needed a true center, and Duckworth’s size made him a better positional fit than Berry. The trade also demonstrates how draft status can obscure development environment. Berry entered the league with greater acclaim, but San Antonio did not create a stable role that offset his weaknesses. Portland’s injuries forced Duckworth into minutes, and the coaching staff allowed him to use his soft shooting touch rather than treating him only as a traditional low-post body. The value difference emerged through fit, patience and role clarity rather than through an obvious talent ranking on trade day. Contract status, health, role congestion and organizational urgency shaped the offers that were realistically available. The retrospective question is whether the front office priced those constraints well enough.

sections.heading: Kevin Duckworth / Walter Berry: Asset Conversion and Opportunity Cost
sections.body: The direct player exchange is decisive. Duckworth gave Portland years of starting production, All-Star seasons, deep playoff runs and a later trade return. Berry gave San Antonio one abbreviated season and no meaningful conversion. No picks or cash complicate the accounting. That simplicity makes the A-plus/F spread unusually defensible. Portland did not merely get the better player; it controlled the player through his prime and then preserved some value at the end. San Antonio’s asset effectively disappeared after 64 games. Draft rights and player control count only when converted into identifiable production or later assets. The ledger is strongest when every major piece is followed to its actual outcome.

sections.heading: Kevin Duckworth / Walter Berry: Verdict and Grade Calibration
sections.body: No verdict or grade change is needed. Blazers Win accurately names the outcome, Portland’s A-plus reflects a two-time All-Star and Finals starter acquired for a short-tenure player, and San Antonio’s F reflects the lack of durable return. The review still matters because it verifies that the original calibration was not based on reputation alone. The canonical record aligns with direct production, years of control, postseason translation and downstream value. This is the benchmark type of clear win that helps calibrate closer trades elsewhere in the database. The verdict separates head-to-head value from team-specific execution. One side can receive a respectable grade and still lose, while A-plus remains reserved for exceptional conversion.

finalVerdict.heading: Final Verdict
finalVerdict.body: Portland wins because Kevin Duckworth became Most Improved Player, a two-time All-Star and the starting center on two Finals teams before yielding later trade value. Walter Berry’s Spurs tenure lasted only 64 games and produced no durable return.
